Quite some years ago, I did some fill-in work for a guitarist of a fairly popular band - but not giant music stars (they just thought they were). This meant spending three months on tour with them and all the mayhem that entailed. But, it was much more recent and covered a bigger geographical area than I was used to playing and the venues were large and much more modern.

It was there on that tour that I discovered some of the larger venues have safe rooms, like you'd see in a house built for wealthy people but larger. That was a novel discovery and there weren't many that had that feature, but they were pretty neat.

Either way, it's pretty cool to see all the ins-and-outs of them and how they operate. These are things that the general public won't ever see. One of the fun things is keeping yourself occupied while you wait for the show. You can wander around, find unlocked doors, and flirt with the concession staff.

Talking to people and getting to know their stories helps me write my lyrics. Most shows where I'm from are in beautiful countryside forests or dirty dirty basements. Not many professional gigs under my belt, just playing.

I've played everywhere from pit parties to house parties to large sport's arenas and fairgrounds or festivals.

It has been a great ride.

I don't do a lot of original stuff, and much prefer the art of faithful replication. I typically found myself (and am again) in high-production cover bands and I enjoy that a great deal. With my background in classical guitar, it makes learning other genres pretty easy. I've enjoyed the broad exposure to the many styles and methods, enjoyed giving people what they expected, and had a great time learning to master the art.

What I really enjoy is the difficulty in getting the studio sound in a live environment. I love the complexity, the variation, and the need to understand more disciplines.

That's my thing, really. It's what I'm passionate about. It's what motivates me to dedicate the many hours to practice. It's also the tool that has enabled me to have some truly fantastic experiences. It's been an awesome life.

Yeah, matching the tone and the sound is almost half of the job, with playing it right the other half. You should write an article one of these days about getting the sound to match the record and how you go about doing that. Is it trial and error? Do you start with the same guitar they use? Do you look up what pedals they used? How do you get the sound right.

I usually try to start with as close to their exact same equipment that they use. I'll often use their specific amps - and then mic those through a second amp. With most artists, you really only need to find the one tone - there's a specific Metallica sound, for example. Once you have it, you don't really have to adjust it much - just find the same effects and settings they themselves used.

It is some trial and error, but there's a bunch of experience that goes into it. Once you've been doing it long enough, it's much easier to do it again and it's much easier to find those you've already found. Like most things, practice improves it. I've spent a lot of time just trying all the various combinations and making mental notes (sometimes physical notes) of what the results are.

This is a great one that bands often overlook. I always scope out the venue and get a tour at least a week prior to the event if I haven't played there before. Sometimes venues will provide a backline, and I need to know if it's suitable so I can plan what gear I need to bring to the stage. If it's a bar/restaurant, I'll sit down and have a drink and or a meal. They're giving me business, so I make it a point to reciprocate.

We're playing larger venues, pretty much exclusively. So, it becomes very important to know the layout and I send the drummer in early to scope things out. I figure he's expendable!

Actually, he's "second in command" and gets paid more because he has additional duties.

Still, it's amazing how many overlook site prep/walk-through. It actually saves time and has the potential to increase safety in the case of an emergency. As I'm playing larger venues with larger crowds, that's something I take very seriously. I feel an obligation, a responsibility, for the safety of my band and my audience. I also want as few distractions as possible and to have a plan that's easily acted on and well communicated.

These are just trivial things - most commonsense. But, they're things I see people not doing.
